works.delta: HyLaT requires training agents specifically to produce and consume hybrid latent-text messages; Relay uses off-the-shelf frozen models with no communication-specific training, observing what notation they spontaneously improvise under a hard budget.

works.title: Emergent Languages in Populations of Language Model Agents: From Token Efficiency to Oversight Evasion
works.what_it_does: Mines a large forum-style dataset of agent interactions for cases where populations of agents invent new notations or languages for token efficiency or oversight evasion, then verifies the inventions are learnable in-context by other models.
works.delta: This is observational, population-scale mining of emergent notation across many adapting agents over many interactions; Relay is a controlled single lineage where one frozen model per turn must inherit and use a notation to solve a certified deduction task, letting notation quality be scored against a sound reference rather than merely detected.

works.title: DMV-Bench: Diagnosing Long-Horizon Multimodal Agents' Visual Memory with Incidental Cue Injection
works.what_it_does: Tests whether a shopping agent recalls a pixel-only cue seen earlier in a chain of autonomous sessions, using a text-leakage contract to keep the signal in pixels alone, and proposes a dual visual+verbal memory architecture (DualMem).
works.delta: DMV-Bench targets one continuous agent's incidental visual recall within an e-commerce task; Relay targets fresh, memoryless instances per turn in a certified deduction game where the image is the entire memory (not an incidental cue atop persistent state), calibrated against a sound baseline.

works.title: Internal vs. External: Comparing Deliberation and Evolution for Multi-Agent Constitutional Design
works.what_it_does: Compares agent-self-deliberated constitutions against externally-evolved rule sets across coordination, public-goods, and trading games; finds evolution beats deliberation in collective-action settings because deliberating agents never propose punishment mechanisms.
works.delta: This 'self-designed underperforms' finding concerns cooperation rule-sets in social-dilemma games; Relay's constitutional-lock-in finding concerns a model pinning its own memory/notation spec for a solo state-tracking task and then being unable to adapt it — rigidity of a self-authored format, not absence of enforcement mechanisms.

works.title: lmgame-Bench: How Good are LLMs at Playing Games?
works.what_it_does: Evaluates LLMs/VLMs on platformer, puzzle, and narrative video games via a unified Gym-style API paired with engineered perception-and-memory scaffolds to stabilize prompt variance across 13 models.
works.delta: lmgame-Bench's memory scaffolds are fixed harness code built to control for prompt sensitivity; Relay's central manipulation is the memory scaffold itself (self-designed baton vs. imposed schema vs. full transcript) and its per-model crossover effects, which lmgame-Bench does not vary or study.

works.title: POPGYM: Benchmarking Partially Observable Reinforcement Learning
works.what_it_does: RL benchmark suite of POMDPs, including a Battleship-style hidden-ship environment, for testing memory-augmented recurrent RL agents.
works.delta: POPGYM agents are trained RL policies with learned recurrent state evaluated over reward; Relay evaluates frozen LLMs with no gradient updates, externalizing memory only through natural language or images across separate instances — a question about substituting text/pixels for weights-based memory that POPGYM cannot pose.

works.title: How Clued up are LLMs? Evaluating Multi-Step Deductive Reasoning in a Text-Based Game Environment
works.what_it_does: Formalizes the Clue board game as multi-step deductive reasoning under partial observability and tests whether a single LLM maintains a logically consistent belief state across turns within its own context.
works.delta: This tests one continuous agent's deductive consistency inside its own persisting context window; Relay removes that continuity entirely (a fresh model, no context) and studies what belief state survives transmission through an externalized, budgeted baton instead.

works.title: Beyond Tokens: A Unified Framework for Latent Communication in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
works.what_it_does: Survey and 3-axis taxonomy of 18 methods (2024-2026) for agents exchanging continuous embeddings, hidden states, or KV-caches instead of text.
works.delta: This surveys latent, sub-symbolic, white-box inter-agent channels; Relay's baton channel is always a black-box, human/model-legible artifact (text or rendered pixels) by construction, since measuring authored external communication — not activation transfer — is the entire point of the benchmark.

threats.title: When LLMs Play the Telephone Game: Cumulative Changes and Attractors in Iterated Cultural Transmissions
threats.overlap: Both study a chain of LLM instances where each link only sees what the previous link produced, and measure how information changes across the chain — the core 'relay of memoryless agents' mechanic (companion threat: LLM as a Broken Telephone, ACL 2025, arXiv:2502.20258, same mechanic via back-translation chains).
threats.differentiation: Telephone-game work passes full, unbounded natural-language text and measures open-ended drift (toxicity, length, factuality) on narrative/translation tasks with no single correct answer. Relay imposes a hard, quantified budget (character count or rendered-pixel bytes) on the passed artifact, plays a certified hidden-information deduction game with a ground-truth-checkable outcome, and scores every budget against a provably-sound, budget-matched belief-tracker baseline to establish which budgets are survivable at all — a ceiling the telephone-game literature has no equivalent of.
threats.claims_to_verify: Confirm neither the ICLR 2025 telephone-game paper nor the ACL 2025 'Broken Telephone' paper impose any explicit size/character/token budget on the inter-agent message (i.e., they pass full outputs unconstrained); confirm neither includes a formally-sound reference compressor/tracker used to certify a budget as information-theoretically sufficient; confirm neither task has a verifiable ground-truth correctness metric (they use toxicity/length/factuality proxies, not solved/unsolved game outcomes).

threats.title: The Vision Wormhole: Latent-Space Communication in Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Systems
threats.overlap: Both repurpose a VLM's visual channel as the bandwidth-constrained bottleneck for transferring memory/state between separate agent instances, explicitly framing it as inter-agent communication through vision.
threats.differentiation: Vision Wormhole injects continuous latent activations directly into the receiver's vision encoder — a white-box, weights-level 'wormhole' requiring instrumented access to both models, with no rendered image ever existing as an intermediate artifact. Relay's baton is a genuine rendered image (or plain text) consumed as ordinary pixel input by a frozen, black-box model instance, so it measures whether a model can author legible external notation for itself, and it is the only one of the two that can observe models defaulting to writing text inside the image rather than inventing spatial/graphical encoding — a phenomenon a latent-injection method cannot surface since there is no rendering step to fail at.
threats.claims_to_verify: Confirm Vision Wormhole's method requires white-box/instrumented access to hidden states or the vision encoder of both sender and receiver models (i.e., cannot be run purely through a commercial chat/vision API); confirm no rendered/rasterized image ever exists as an intermediate artifact in their pipeline (the 'communication' is activation-level, not pixel-level); confirm they report no findings about spontaneous notation choice (text-in-image vs. spatial/diagrammatic encoding), since their channel bypasses rendering entirely.

threats.title: Glyph: Scaling Context Windows via Visual-Text Compression
threats.overlap: Both treat 'render text to pixels' as a bandwidth-saving channel and study a fidelity/compression tradeoff as the budget (compression ratio / image size) shrinks, including OCR-style read-back of the rendered content (companion threat: DeepSeek-OCR, arXiv:2510.18234, same optical-compression idea with explicit OCR-precision-vs-ratio curves).
threats.differentiation: Glyph/DeepSeek-OCR compress a single model's own existing long context for efficiency within one continuous inference session, measured by downstream QA accuracy or OCR decoding precision on statically rendered documents. Relay uses the rendered image as the ONLY memory bridge between independently-instantiated models across turns of a live deduction game, and its key finding is that read-back fidelity (can the next instance OCR its own prior notation) dissociates from game performance (getting the notation right doesn't predict winning) — a distinction that requires the multi-instance relay setup and does not arise when a single continuous session compresses its own context.
threats.claims_to_verify: Confirm Glyph and DeepSeek-OCR evaluate a single model/pipeline reading back text it rendered within the same session or task, not text authored by a prior, separate model instance with no shared parameters or context; confirm their headline accuracy metrics are direct QA/OCR correctness rather than a downstream multi-turn game outcome that could diverge from OCR fidelity; confirm neither paper reports cases where near-perfect OCR read-back coexists with downstream task failure (the fidelity/performance dissociation Relay reports).

verdicts.evidence:
Verified against arXiv:2605.30785 abstract (via WebFetch) and the raw HTML full text (fetched with curl, tags stripped, then grepped directly — not relying on any summarizer's paraphrase for the load-bearing negatives).

(a) Crossover is about agent capability/strength, not schema authorship. Verbatim (§4.4): "Using vanilla ReAct performance as a proxy for agent capability, stronger agents such as GLM and Qwen can exploit longer raw contexts, so AdaCoM intervenes later and more lightly; weaker agents such as DeepSeek and Kimi benefit from shorter, distilled contexts, so AdaCoM compresses more frequently. This reflects a balance between fidelity and reliability: preserving raw trajectories retains fine-grained evidence, but beyond an agent's effective context length, additional raw content can harm reasoning." Also: "agents with higher vanilla ReAct performance benefit from higher-fidelity context preservation, whereas lower-performing agents require more aggressive compression to stay wit[hin reliable range]." This comparison holds the mechanism constant (an externally-trained AdaCoM manager in all cases) and varies only which agent (i.e., its capability level) is being managed — it is not a comparison of self-authored vs. externally-imposed schema.

(b) No "self-authored schema" condition exists. Direct grep of the raw stripped text for "self-authored", "self-design(ed)", "sound", and "certifi*" all returned zero hits. "Schema" appears exactly once, referring to the manager's JSON "output schema" for its action format — an implementation detail, not a self-designed-vs-imposed memory-structure axis. The paper does contain adjacent but distinct "self-management" baselines, MemAct and SumAgent (table row "CM Model: agent itself"), where the agent executes its own pruning/summarization via a fixed, predefined operation ("the agent can invoke a prune tool to summarize selected historical messages, remove them, and append the generated summary"; "the agent conditions on the original question, previous summary, and latest tool interaction to update the summary"). These are ablations on WHO EXECUTES a fixed compression operation, not on who DESIGNS the context's structure/schema, and the paper's own diagnosis of their instability is unrelated to schema design: "This supports the hypothesis that asking the agent to manage its own context may require agent-side training, since the resulting summaries may not be reliably usable by the original agent." Critically, this self- vs. external-execution ablation is never invoked to explain the Fidelity-Reliability crossover (part a) — that finding is generated entirely within the AdaCoM (externally-managed) condition, varying agent capability, not management-authorship.

(c) No sound/certified reference floor. Confirmed via the same zero-hit grep for "sound" / "certifi*" across the full raw text. AdaCoM's baselines are ReAct (no management), SumAgent, MemAct (self-management), SumCoM (fixed external summarization), and AdaCoM w/o training — none is framed as a provably-sound or certified truncation floor. The only budget-like constraints found are soft, RL-shaped, token-based: "we set the manager's own input context-window length to 32,768 tokens and its maximum output length to 4,096 tokens" plus "If the managed context exceeds the given context length limit, we apply a token penalty to the manager step that produced the over-length context" — an RL training penalty, not a hard enforced or certified budget, and the paper is text-only (no pixel budget concept at all).

Differentiation confirmed: the "manager" is explicitly "an external LLM" trained via "end-to-end reinforcement learning" while "keeping the agent frozen," operating as "before each agent step, the manager updates the running context, and the agent then acts on the resulting managed context" — i.e., one continuously-growing session under a frozen agent, with no language anywhere in the text about severance into independently-sampled fresh instances/episodes (grep for "fresh", "independently sampled", "sever*" in relevant context found nothing matching that concept; the one "fresh" hit concerned held-out task-generation topic diversity, unrelated to episode severance). The crossover axis is explicitly compression aggressiveness/frequency ("AdaCoM intervenes later and more lightly" vs. "AdaCoM compresses more frequently") tied to agent capability, not who designs the schema.

Access: WebFetch of https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30785 confirmed title/authors/abstract match ("Learning Agent-Compatible Context Management for Long-Horizon Tasks," Lu Yi et al., introducing "Adaptive Context Management (AdaCoM)... trains an external LLM to manage frozen agent context... Fidelity-Reliability Trade-off"). Full text fetched from https://arxiv.org/html/2605.30785v1 via curl, HTML tags stripped locally, and all quotes above verified by direct grep against that raw stripped text (not the WebFetch summarizer's paraphrase) to guard against convenient-but-inexact quotes.

Both papers verified via WebFetch of arxiv.org/abs and arxiv.org/html full text (2410.08948 "Emergent Social Conventions and Collective Bias in LLM Populations", Ashery/Aiello/Baronchelli; 2606.04197 "Exploring the Topology and Memory of Consensus: How LLM Agents Agree, Fragment, or Settle When Forming Conventions", Mehdizadeh/Hilbert, submitted 2 Jun 2026, target JASSS).

1) MEMORY FORMAT — neither "raw transcript" nor "authored artifact"; it's a system-maintained structured log:
- Paper 1 (2410.08948): "the prompt provides the LLM agent with a 'memory' storing details about the past H interactions they participated in, including their co-player's convention choice, their own convention choice, whether the interaction was successful or not, and their own accumulated score" — with "we set the name pool size to W=10 and the individual memory length to H=5 for populations of N=24 agents."
- Paper 2 (2606.04197), Sec 2.1/2.2: "Each memory entry stores the agent's previous choice, its partner's choice, and whether the interaction succeeded," implemented as "a fixed-size first-in, first-out deque," rendered in-prompt as e.g. "Interaction 1: You chose: M, Partner chose: Y, Success: No." Memory depth tested at M ∈ {2, 5, 10}.
So memory depth = a bounded FIFO of structured outcome tuples (choice/partner-choice/success[/score]), not uncompressed dialogue and not an agent-authored/compressed artifact. This is a third category the either/or framing in the task didn't anticipate, but it does NOT contradict our differentiation text (which only says "rolling memory window," not "raw transcript") — it actually reinforces the contrast, since their memory is auto-populated bookkeeping rather than anything the agent itself composes under a budget.

2) INDIVIDUAL-AGENT DRIFT/MUTATION — absent in both papers, confirmed by direct search:
- Names/conventions are drawn from "a name pool of finite size W... presented to them as a list of W unique letters sampled from the English alphabet" (paper 1) or a fixed letter set (paper 2: C, D, F, J, M, P, Q, R, X, Y) — agents select from this fixed pool, they do not invent novel conventions.
- No passage in either full text discusses a single agent's own convention/word meaning drifting, mutating, or evolving over successive interactions. Both papers' unit of analysis is population-level: consensus emergence, fragmentation, collective bias, critical-mass/committed-minority effects (paper 1), and network-position effects like "brokerage penalty" for high-betweenness bridge agents (paper 2) — never within-agent semantic drift of an invented notation.
- This directly confirms there is no precedent in this paper family for a single-model within-episode notation-drift claim.

3) POPULATION SIZES / ROUNDS — matches the claimed "16-200 agents" range:
- Paper 1: primary experiments N=24; robustness and critical-mass checks extend to N=48 and N=200 ("populations as large as N=200 agents reach consensus... for a name pool as large as W=26"); consensus reported by "population round 15 in all cases, except for Llama-2-70b-Chat"; committed-minority experiments run up to 30 population rounds to find the critical-mass threshold.
- Paper 2: exactly 16 agents per topology, "eight fixed 16-agent topologies," 432 total simulation runs, memory depth M ∈ {2,5,10}, "Simulations were run for a maximum of 1,600 rounds, corresponding to 100 population cycles," with observed settling times "approximately 190–926 rounds" depending on condition.
- Minor residual gap: the precise operational definition of one "population round" in paper 1 (single pairwise draw vs. an N-normalized cycle) was not locatable in the extracted text — a documentation gap in the source paper itself, not a defect in our claim; flagging for caution if exact round-to-round comparisons are made downstream.

4) IMAGE/PIXEL CHANNEL VARIANT — none found. Both papers use only abstract letter symbols for the naming game; explicit search of paper 2's full text confirmed "no visual or pixel-based variant discussed," and no such variant surfaced anywhere in paper 1 either.

Net: every specific factual claim in the verification request checks out against full text, and the stated differentiation (population-scale persistent agents with rolling memory across many pairwise rounds; no hard externalization budget forcing single-artifact compression; no certified sound-reference floor; object of study is population consensus/bias, not one model's own hand-off encoding) is not contradicted anywhere in either paper.

Read the full 23-page PDF (arXiv:2606.19857, "Large Language Models Do Not Always Need Readable Language," fetched via arxiv.org/pdf/2606.19857 and extracted with pdftotext; abstract-page fetch initially hit a stale CDN cache showing an unrelated paper, re-fetched with cache-bust and confirmed correct title/ID match). Findings on both sub-claims:

(1) Elicitation, not spontaneous/unprompted emergence in an agentic task:
- Abstract itself: "We refer to this class of model-centric textual representations as BabelTele, approached here not as a fixed protocol but as an empirical probe into LLMs' capacity to generate and interpret such representations. Through readability diagnostics, model likelihood measures, human questionnaires, and downstream task evaluations..." — i.e., the paradigm is directly probed/elicited, exactly as our differentiation states.
- Methodology section: "By applying these constraints through zero-shot prompting, we encourage LLMs to externalize semantic information into a compact surface form more effectively."
- Appendix C.1 gives the literal elicitation prompt: "your task: compress verbose human text into minimal Token sequence. Audience ≠ human, but another equally intelligent LLM. Core Directive: Omnilingual... Symbolic Collapse... Universality... Lossless... Compress the content bellow:" — a direct compression instruction, not something arising as a side effect of trying to win a game.
- Section 4.3 explicitly: "We contrast simply prompt-elicited BabelTele representations with standard abstractive summaries and a carefully engineered extractive baseline (LLMLingua-2)."
- The paper even runs 13 explicit prompt variants (Table 6, "BabelTele-like prompt variants") to show the phenomenon is a "family" reachable via many instructions — reinforcing that it is instruction-driven, not spontaneous task pressure. The one bullet that uses the word "spontaneously" ("by removing human readability as a default constraint, LLMs spontaneously produce opaque... representations under a black-box interface") describes the model's autonomous choice of *surface form* once the readability constraint is explicitly lifted by prompt — not unprompted emergence during a hidden-state game.

(2) Agent memory / multi-agent communication have no hidden ground-truth state a receiver must reconstruct, and no certified-sound-baseline budget:
- LoCoMo (agent memory) is described as: "used as an initial testbed for long-term conversational memory compression. Instead of compressing isolated passages, this setting compresses dialogue histories or memory contexts before answering memory dependent questions. The goal is to test whether BabelTele can reduce agent memory storage while preserving enough reliable information for downstream recall." Appendix E.4.1 confirms the mechanics: compress each session → retrieve top-4 similar sessions by embedding similarity → answer, graded by GPT-4o-mini against reference answers (Table 4: Token count, Acc., % vs. uncompressed). This is a retrieval-QA fidelity benchmark over shared/known conversational content, not a hidden-state deduction game.
- Multi-agent communication uses DeepResearch Bench: "We built a multi-agent system consisting of two agents and tested it on the DeepResearch Bench (Du et al., 2025a)... intermediate messages between agents are compressed before being passed to the next agent." Table 3 grades it by "Token Reduction" and "Score" (% of uncompressed baseline) in homogeneous/heterogeneous settings — a task-quality score relative to an uncompressed baseline, not an outcome graded against a provably sound/certified reference tracker or information floor.
- The metrics section (B.5) states plainly: "System Utility. For agent memory and multi-agent communication, we focus on operational metrics in realistic interactive settings: context token reduction, task accuracy or success rate, and, where available, response or reasoning-token overhead." No mention anywhere of a certified/provably-sound baseline or an information-theoretic floor for these settings.
- A full-text search for "hidden," "ground truth state," "deduction," "guess" found zero task-design occurrences — the only "hidden" hits concern "hidden states" of model internals in the unrelated-work discussion of activation-based compression, not a hidden game state a receiver must reconstruct.

Both our claims about the paper and our differentiation from a hidden-state deduction game with a certified/sound baseline survive full-text scrutiny; nothing in the 23-page paper (main text or appendices) contradicts them.

Memory architecture is the variable the framework leaves out."

Self-Spec's per-task code artifact (the "WorkingSpec") is genuinely single-shot: it is instantiated once from a problem's docstring/signature and consumed in exactly one deterministic (T=0), single-sample code generation, with no reranking or repeated sampling (pass@1 only) — confirmed verbatim in the paper. However, do not claim the paper establishes that Self-Spec's artifact overall is "authored once and consumed once" with "no repeated reuse across many subsequent turns" without qualification: the paper is explicitly ambiguous about whether the model-authored *schema/notation* itself (the "GlobalSPEC," e.g. "CUE-Spec v1.0" in Fig. 1) is freshly authored per HumanEval task or created once and reused/pinned across all 164 tasks per model — Section 3 says only that it is "created once per session" without defining session boundaries, and the paper's own AI correctness reviewer flagged this exact ambiguity as unresolved and reproducibility-relevant. State the differentiation as: the task-level spec-to-code pass is single-shot and confirmed; whether the schema-level notation is reused across the benchmark's many tasks is not established either way by the paper.

The reported effect sizes (GPT-4o 87%→92% +5, Claude 3.7 92%→94% +2, Claude 3.5 90%→89% −1) are accurate — they match verbatim between abstract and Table 1 — and are not cherry-picked, since all three tested models' outcomes (including the one regression) are disclosed. No ablation in the paper tests iterated reuse of one pinned spec across multiple generations — confirmed. The paper contains no ablations of any kind (a gap its own reviewer names explicitly), only the single pass@1/T=0 comparison. This supports the claim that Self-Spec's design and evaluation never probe the repeated-reuse/lock-in regime — but frame it as "the paper does not test this scenario," not as "the paper's design rules this scenario out," since the schema-reuse-across-164-tasks ambiguity in (a) means the closest analogue to repeated reuse may already be latent, untested, in the base experimental design itself.
